content: A walker, also known as a walking frame, is a mobility aid designed for individuals with disabilities or those who require additional support to maintain balance and stability while walking. It typically consists of a frame that is approximately waist-high, about twelve inches deep, and slightly wider than the user. Walkers are available in various sizes, including pediatric models for children and bariatric models for overweight or obese individuals. Modern walkers are adjustable in height and should be set to a level that allows the user to maintain a slight bend in their arms. This arm bend is essential for proper blood circulation during use. The front two legs of a walker may or may not have wheels, depending on the user’s strength and abilities. Some walkers with front wheels also feature caster wheels or glides on the back legs to facilitate movement. When using a walker, the individual positions the frame around their front and sides, holding onto the top of the frame for support. Traditional walkers are lifted and placed a short distance ahead, after which the user walks to the frame and repeats the process. Walkers equipped with wheels and glides can be pushed forward instead of being lifted, making them easier to use, especially for individuals with limited arm strength. Walkers are particularly beneficial for those recovering from leg or back injuries, as well as individuals with walking difficulties or mild balance issues. A related device is the hemi-walker, which is about half the size of a traditional walker. It is designed for individuals with limited or no dexterity in one hand or arm. Hemi-walkers offer greater stability than a quad cane (a cane with four ground contact points) but are generally not as highly recommended as traditional walkers for those who can use them. A wheeled walker, commonly referred to as a rollator, is a walking frame equipped with wheels. Modern rollators are more advanced than conventional wheeled walkers. They are height-adjustable and often include features such as a seat and, in some cases, a basket. Made from lightweight yet durable materials, modern rollators may also have a backrest for added support. A key feature of rollators is the inclusion of hand brakes mounted on the top of the frame. These brakes can be lifted or pushed downward to stop the rollator immediately. They can also assist in maneuvering, as braking on one side during a turn allows for a tighter turning radius. Rollators with wheels at least seven inches in diameter, preferably eight inches, provide better reliability. For enhanced safety, convenience, and durability, modern rollators often include tubular seats, backrests, and baskets with spacers and cushions. Instead of simple hooks, they are equipped with latches and release buttons for secure attachment and ease of use. In British English, the term Zimmer frame is commonly used to refer to a walker. This name originates from Zimmer Holdings, a prominent manufacturer of mobility aids and joint replacement components. In May 2007, a group of elderly individuals in the UK formed a rock band called The Zimmers to raise awareness about the challenges associated with aging. The band’s name was inspired by this generic term for walkers.
